meta.titre: Insect-Pollinated and Wind-Pollinated Flowers: A Point-by-Point Comparison
meta.sous_theme: Flower adaptations for insect pollination and wind pollination

sections.contenu_markdown:
A hibiscus hedge in a compound is busy with bees and butterflies, while a maize field nearby has plain flowers that nobody notices.
Both kinds of plant need pollen to reach the stigma, but they use different agents and so have very different flowers.
GCE Biology has repeatedly asked candidates to compare the two kinds of flower and to name the part that does each job.
This course shows the features side by side so that you can give a mark-winning answer.

items: A flower has sepals, petals, stamens (anther and filament) and a carpel (stigma, style and ovary).
Pollen grains contain the male gametes of a flowering plant.
Fertilization is the fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete.

sections.titre: Pollination and the two kinds of flower
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Pollination
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. It is not fertilization: fertilization happens later, after the pollen has grown a tube. The pollen may reach a flower on the same plant (self-pollination) or on another plant of the same species (cross-pollination). The agents are mainly insects and wind.

### How an insect carries pollen
An insect visits a flower for nectar or pollen. The anthers touch its body and some pollen sticks to it. At the next flower it brushes against the stigma and leaves some pollen there.

### Insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers

| Part | Insect-pollinated flower | Wind-pollinated flower |
|---|---|---|
| Petals | Large, brightly coloured to attract insects | Small, dull or green, or absent |
| Scent and nectar | Often scented; nectaries make nectar | No scent and no nectar |
| Anthers | Inside the flower, firmly attached | Hang outside the flower on long filaments, loosely attached so wind shakes them |
| Pollen | Smaller amount; grains sticky or spiny | Very large amount; grains small, light and smooth |
| Stigma | Small and sticky, inside the flower | Large and feathery, hanging outside to catch pollen from the air |

A hibiscus flower has large coloured petals; these are the part that attracts insects. Examples of wind-pollinated plants are maize and grasses.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for differences
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give one row of the table per mark, with both sides: 'An insect-pollinated flower has large coloured petals, but a wind-pollinated flower has small dull petals.'

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a feature is named and the reason is asked
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name the feature, then link it to the agent. Feathery stigmas have a large surface that catches pollen from the air.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the amount of pollen is compared
variantes.contenu_markdown: Wind carries pollen at random, so most grains never reach a stigma; the plant makes very many. An insect travels straight from flower to flower, so less pollen is wasted.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Flower P has bright yellow petals, a sweet smell and anthers inside the flower. Flower Q has small green petals, long filaments that carry the anthers outside and a feathery stigma.

(a) Which flower is pollinated by wind?

(b) Give two features of Q that suit wind pollination.

(c) Explain why Q produces far more pollen than P.

etapes.action: List the clues for each flower.
etapes.justification: Colour, scent and position of anthers point to the agent.
etapes.resultat_markdown: P: coloured, scented, anthers inside. Q: green, anthers outside, feathery stigma.

etapes.action: Match the clues to the agent.
etapes.justification: Bright petals and scent attract insects; dull petals and exposed parts suit wind.
etapes.resultat_markdown: P is insect-pollinated; Q is wind-pollinated.

etapes.action: Pick two features of Q and give the use of each.
etapes.justification: A marked answer links the feature to wind.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Anthers outside, so wind can shake pollen away; feathery stigma, so it catches pollen.

etapes.justification: Wind carries grains in any direction, so most are wasted.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Many grains are made so that some reach a stigma.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) **Flower Q.** (b) **Anthers hang outside on long filaments** and **the stigma is feathery.** (c) **Wind blows pollen at random, so most grains miss a stigma; a large amount makes a hit likely.**

items.erreur_markdown: Pollination is the fusion of the male and female gametes.
items.pourquoi_faux: That is fertilization. Pollination is only the transfer of pollen to the stigma.
items.correction_markdown: Pollination: pollen from anther to stigma. Fertilization: gametes fuse after the pollen tube grows.

items.erreur_markdown: A wind-pollinated flower has bright petals and nectar.
items.pourquoi_faux: Wind needs no attraction. Bright petals and nectar are for insects.
items.correction_markdown: Wind-pollinated flowers have small dull petals and no nectar.

items.pourquoi_faux: A feathery stigma hangs outside the flower to catch pollen from the air. Insect-pollinated flowers have small, sticky stigmas inside the flower.
items.correction_markdown: Insect-pollinated: small sticky stigma. Wind-pollinated: large feathery stigma.

items.erreur_markdown: Only one flower is described, for example 'It has large coloured petals'.
items.pourquoi_faux: A difference needs both sides, otherwise the examiner cannot tell the contrast.
items.correction_markdown: 'Large coloured petals, but the other flower has small dull petals.'

items.erreur_markdown: Wind-pollinated flowers make little pollen because the wind carries it a long way.
items.pourquoi_faux: Wind carries pollen at random and many grains are lost.
items.correction_markdown: Wind-pollinated flowers make a very large amount of pollen.

items.enonce_markdown: In a hibiscus flower, name the part (a) that attracts insects, (b) that produces pollen, (c) that receives pollen.
A grass flower is pollinated by wind. Give **four** features that suit wind pollination, and the reason for each.
items.solution_markdown:
Any four of:

- Anthers hang outside on long filaments, so wind can shake out the pollen.
- Very large amount of pollen, because many grains are lost.
- Pollen grains small, light and smooth, so wind carries them far.
- Stigma large and feathery and outside the flower, so it catches pollen from the air.
- Small dull petals, because there is no need to attract insects.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student wants to show that insects are needed for fruit formation in a plant that has insect-pollinated flowers. She covers 20 young flowers with fine mesh bags before they open and leaves 20 similar flowers uncovered. Later, 3 covered flowers and 17 uncovered flowers form fruits.

(a) Why does she use mesh and not plastic?

(b) Calculate the percentage of fruit formation in each group.

(c) State the conclusion and one factor she must keep the same.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Mesh lets air and light through but keeps insects out. Plastic would change other conditions such as air and temperature.

(b) Covered: 3 / 20 x 100 = **15%**. Uncovered: 17 / 20 x 100 = **85%**.

(c) Fruit formation is much greater when insects can visit the flowers, so insects are needed (a difference of 70 percentage points). The flowers must be the same species and age, and receive the same light and water. The few fruits in the covered group may come from self-pollination or from pollen already on the stigma.

items_markdown: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; fertilization is a later stage.
Insect-pollinated flowers: large coloured scented petals, nectar, anthers and small sticky stigma inside, sticky or spiny pollen in smaller amounts.
Wind-pollinated flowers: small dull petals, no scent or nectar, anthers and large feathery stigma hanging outside, large amounts of light pollen.
Wind carries pollen at random, so the plant makes much more of it.
In a 'differentiate' answer, put both flowers in every sentence.
